chief_complaint: severe abdominal swelling, peripheral edema, elevated jugular pressure, and Kussmaul sign
hpi_details: 57M with history of remote tuberculous pericarditis presenting with right heart failure symptoms, Kussmaul sign, pericardial calcification on CT, and equalization of diastolic pressures requiring radical pericardiectomy.
ideas: He thinks his liver or kidneys are shutting down because fluid is backing up heavily into his stomach and legs.
concerns: He is worried that this sudden abdominal fluid means he has incurable liver cancer like his older brother had.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will drain the fluid from his belly today and prescribe high-dose water pills so his clothes fit again.

available_results.value: Diffuse calcified pericardial thickening up to 8 mm encasing both ventricles
Near-equal right- and left-ventricular end-diastolic pressures at 24 and 26 mmHg with dip-and-plateau waveforms

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Constrictive Pericarditis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Definitive treatment is surgical radical pericardiectomy; medical therapy (diuretics) offers only temporary symptomatic relief and does not reverse the fixed restriction.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe abdominal swelling, peripheral edema, elevated jugular pressure, and Kussmaul sign

Key HPI features: 57M with history of remote tuberculous pericarditis presenting with right heart failure symptoms, Kussmaul sign, pericardial calcification on CT, and equalization of diastolic pressures requiring radical pericardiectomy.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Constrictive Pericarditis Pericardiectomy.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Constrictive Pericarditis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Restrictive cardiomyopathy without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly worsening ascites unresponsive to diuretics — signals need for definitive surgical treatment.
management_principles: Confirm with echocardiography/CT/MRI showing pericardial thickening or calcification and septal bounce; cardiac catheterization to demonstrate equalization of diastolic pressures
Refer to cardiothoracic surgery for pericardiectomy once diagnosis is confirmed; diuretics can bridge symptoms but are not curative
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: A rigid, thickened, often calcified pericardium — commonly from remote tuberculous infection — prevents the heart from filling normally, causing right heart failure symptoms and Kussmaul's sign, treated definitively with surgical pericardiectomy.
differentials: Right ventricular failure from another cause
red_flags: Rapidly worsening ascites unresponsive to diuretics — signals need for definitive surgical treatment

must_ask.say: Have you ever had tuberculosis, especially involving your lungs or the sac around your heart?
Where is the swelling — your belly and legs?
Has anyone noticed the veins in your neck are more prominent?
How has this been progressing over time?
How is your energy and ability to exercise?

history.answer: My stomach has become terribly swollen and tight over the past few months, and now both of my legs and feet are swollen too.
It started mainly in my belly, but over the last couple of months, both of my lower legs, ankles, and feet have become very puffy as well.
The swelling came on gradually over the past four to six months, but it has been getting noticeably worse over the last few weeks.
The leg swelling tends to get a bit worse toward the evening, but my swollen abdomen stays tight and distended all day and night.
Yes, when I press on my shins or take off my socks at night, there are deep indents that take several minutes to disappear.
I have gained about six kilograms over the last two months, even though I haven't been eating more food.
No, neither leg is red, hot, or painful to touch; they just feel heavy and tight.
I get winded when walking up stairs or doing chores, but I can sleep flat without needing extra pillows, and I don't wake up gasping.
Yes, I feel exhausted very easily lately. I used to be quite active, but now even walking a short distance wears me out completely.
Yes, actually, I noticed the veins on the sides of my neck look bulging and prominent when I look in the mirror.
No, my urine looks normal in color with no foam or blood, though the amount feels slightly less than usual.
No yellowing of my eyes or skin, and I haven't noticed any unusual bruising or bleeding.
About twenty years ago, I was treated for tuberculosis that affected the sac around my heart, and I took medication for nine months.
No, I haven't had any recent sore throat, fever, or skin infections at all.
No cold sensitivity, hair loss, or severe constipation; my bowel movements are pretty regular.
My appetite is actually somewhat decreased because my stomach feels full and bloated so quickly, but I have no chronic diarrhea.
No, I haven't had any recent long flights, bed rest, or recent surgeries.
I try to keep my salt intake moderate, and I don't stand for prolonged hours at work.
I have high blood pressure and mild high cholesterol, both diagnosed about five years ago.
No surgeries. I was hospitalized briefly twenty years ago when I was treated for the tuberculous pericarditis.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once a day for my blood pressure. I don't take any pain relievers, steroids, or other supplements.
I don't have any known drug allergies.
I have never smoked in my life.
I rarely drink, maybe one glass of wine on a special occasion, and I've never had hepatitis.
I work as an office manager and live with my wife in an apartment.
My father had high blood pressure, but there is no family history of heart failure, liver disease, or kidney failure.

I thought maybe my kidneys or liver had stopped working properly because all this fluid keeps building up in my belly and legs. I'm really frightened this swelling means I have liver cancer, which is the same thing that took my older brother.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, and body temperature 36.6°C.
Marked jugular venous distension up to the jaw angle at 45 degrees, with a paradoxical rise in jugular pressure during inspiration consistent with Kussmaul sign.
Regular heart sounds with an early diastolic sound consistent with a pericardial knock along the left lower sternal border, but no murmurs or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without crackles, rales, or wheezes.
Markedly distended and protuberant abdomen without surgical scars or prominent venous collaterals.
Flank dullness with positive shifting dullness and fluid wave, consistent with moderate-to-severe ascites.
Smooth, tender hepatomegaly palpated 4 cm below the right costal margin without splenomegaly.
Symmetric 3+ pitting edema present over both lower legs and extending up to the mid-shins bilaterally.
Bilateral calves are equal in circumference without localized warmth, erythema, or cord-like tenderness.
Normal skin turgor with no spider angiomas, palmar erythema, jaundice, or petechiae.
Thyroid gland is normal in size and texture without nodules, enlargement, or tenderness.
